rv.q: The production is rather too ridiculous to become the tear-jerker it could be but it's enjoyable nevertheless.
These performers know how to sell a song, but there’s so much more that needs fixing here.
It gives Dark of the Moon a strong emotional core, which, along with its memorable aesthetics and musical style, means it leaves a powerful impression.
An engaging and eclectic production that held my attention throughout.

John, one of the witches, crosses into the human realm and challenges Barbara’s boyfriend to a rather unequal duel. Using his magic powers, John flings his rival into the dirt and then proposes to Barbara. But John can’t shake off the Witch People, who stalk him from the shadows, cursing him as a deserter and hoping that his marriage will fail.
Adamson and Jones carry John and Barbara’s high-stakes forbidden romance with rich vocal harmonies and an intoxicating chemistry sure to appeal to romantasy fans.
It just about works, but other aspects of this supernatural show are less successful.
It makes for an enjoyable and engaging evening, if not a ground-breaking one, feeling particularly well-suited to smaller theatre spaces.

So, go for the agonies of forbidden love and the singing and chemistry of the two leads delivering a pleasant score, but don’t expect narrative depth and don’t think too hard about mysteriously powerful men bewitching young women, be they strongminded or not.
But despite all the smoke, shadows and strained yearning, Dark of the Moon never quite finds the pulse it’s searching for.
Dark of the Moon is a case of strong ideas undone by inconsistent execution.
The tickets are extremely affordable, which is very commendable, there are some fantastic production elements, and the cast performances are sublime.

While the score made an admirable attempt to blend its contrasting musical influences, the majority of the songs commented on the action rather than advancing the narrative or deepening character development.
All told, Dark of the Moon feels like it is missing that spark that can turn a good idea into a great musical.

The style in which it has been made has ultimately fought back against that grounding, and the show ultimately doesn’t really find the balance between humour, style and content that it needs to take it to the next level.
It is rare that a musical wastes its potential so spectacularly.

cn.t: Mixed reception for this supernatural Appalachian musical, with critics praising Georgie Rankcom's fluid direction and staging but criticizing an inert, clichéd story that struggles to generate dramatic heat despite intriguing folklore origins.
